gap: No result ChatGPT got says what a laptop actually gets from the Anker Prime 100W (A2688) once a second device is plugged in: Anker's own spec sheet gives 65 W to the laptop on USB-C1 when both USB-C ports are used (65 W + 35 W), and only 12 W when the laptop is on USB-C2 with a phone on USB-A (12 W + 12 W).
standout_why: I compared against the cited/top Anker pages. The A2688 US page (the charger ChatGPT recommended for 'charging multiple devices') only says 'Two Ports in Use: 100W Max' and 'Three Ports in Use: 89W Max', with no per-port split, plus a footnote to 'use the upper port for charging laptops'. The A121B page does publish its own split (70 W + 30 W, or 95 W + 5 W), so rivals have the idea but not for the product ChatGPT picked. The A120F page is a single-port charger and has no split. None of these pages states the 65 W ceiling or the 12 W C2+A trap for the A2688.
decides: This confirms that a '100 W' multi-port charger is really a 65 W laptop charger once you also charge a phone from it. A shopper whose laptop needs close to 100 W while sharing the charger should look at the higher-wattage UGREEN/Anker 140–200 W models already listed. A shopper with a 65 W laptop is fine with the A2688 if the laptop goes on the top port. The table footnote should be: 'laptop watts with a phone also plugged in', not the headline total.
